extracted.intended_audience: historians and chronologists of ancient Mediterranean and biblical periods; scholars reconstructing ancient chronologies
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for constructing and reconciling chronologies of ancient Mediterranean (Hebrew, Egyptian, Phoenician, Greek) events by using synchronisms, reign-lengths, Olympiad anchors, and critical evaluation of ancient authorities. Emphasises proportional corrections, generation-counting, and weighing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-cultural synchronisms to fix dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix dates by synchronizing events and movements across different peoples (e.g., Phoenician colonies, the flight of the Zidonians, the Argonautic expedition) with the reigns of known kings (David, Solomon, Rehoboam) and Greek events (Trojan war, Olympiads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text include fixing Phoenician colonisations to the fifteenth or sixteenth year of David's reign, placing the Argonautic expedition about 43 years after Solomon's death, and dating Troy's fall about 76–78 years after Solomon. Use movements of peoples, foundation of cities, and mutual references in ancient authors as synchronising evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer earlier, less-corrupted authorities where available
rubrics_metrics.description: Give greater weight to testimonies of earlier authors who wrote before later corruptions (e.g., "by the Testimony of both Homer and Hesiod, who wrote before the Greeks and Egyptians corrupted their Antiquities").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites Homer and Hesiod as evidence for relative sequencing (e.g., Bacchus older than the Argonauts). Where annals or translations of Phoenician histories exist (Menander of Pergamus translating Tyrian annals), these contemporary or earlier records should be used preferentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor chronology to secure fixed events (Olympiads, conquests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use securely datable benchmarks — such as Olympiads and well-attested conquests (e.g., Cyrus's taking of Sardes and Babylon) — as anchor points for counting backwards or forwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text anchors many computations to 'An. 4, Olymp. 60' (Cyrus taking Babylon) and uses the Olympiad system to position Solon, Draco, and other Greek legislators and events relative to Solomon's death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reign-lengths and generational counts but correct inflated totals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reckon dates by adding reign-lengths or generations, but be prepared to shorten or adjust those totals when they are collected 'equipollent to Generations' or otherwise inflated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends shortening the 'Marbles' reckoning in the proportion of four to seven for periods before Cyrus to approach truth, and gives examples where 54 years shortened proportionally become 31 years. Do not accept long aggregated reign totals uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select realistic generation/reign lengths and apply consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose plausible average lengths for generations or reigns (e.g., 27 years to a generation; 19 years a-piece for certain Athenian kings) and use them to compute intervals, adjusting where institutional practices differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: counting nine intervals at 27 years to place the Return of the Heraclides; assuming 19 years per Athenian king, 14–15 years per life-archon, and decennial archons usually reckoned at seventy years but possibly shorter if deaths occurred. Be explicit about the chosen average and show its arithmetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional norms (types of magistracies) to estimate durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate periods by reference to the normative lengths of offices (e.g., Olympic presidencies, archons for life, decennial archons) and adjust for irregularities or mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text models Athenian succession as eight kings at ~19 years each, then twelve life-archons at 14–15 years, then seven decennial archons usually totaled at 70 years but plausibly shorter. Use these institutional norms as working estimates but allow variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply proportional correction methods when reconciling competing chronologies
rubrics_metrics.description: When large chronological systems (e.g., the 'Marbles') conflict with other anchors, apply a stated proportional correction (here: shorten earlier reign totals in proportion 4:7) to reconcile them with better-attested fixed dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book demonstrates subtracting proportionally shortened intervals from a fixed Olympiad date to reposition events (e.g., moving the Conquest of Cirrha from An. 2, Olymp. 47 to An. 1, Olymp. 53 after correction). Explicitly state and justify the correction factor used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically assess poetic and mythic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat epic poets and mythographers (Homer, Hesiod, legends of Bacchus/Hercules/Argonauts) cautiously: they can provide relative sequencing but are not straightforward chronological records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses Homer and Hesiod for relative ordering (e.g., Bacchus one generation older than the Argonauts) but rejects taking them as direct evidence for earlier navigation or precise years. Use myths for plausibility and cross-check with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use migration, colonisation, and technological diffusion as chronological indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlate the spread of seafaring, colonies, and maritime technology (e.g., long ships, triremes) with chronological phases to date when peoples began new types of voyaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Phoenician/Zidonian migration after David's victories leading to Mediterranean colonisation; Tyrians' shift from Red Sea to Mediterranean trade after Edom's revolt; Corinthians building triremes ~300 years before the end of the Peloponnesian war. Use archaeological and literary evidence of trade/colonies as time markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for possible contemporaneity or non-sequential successions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that founders or named figures (e.g., Caranus and Perdiccas) may have been contemporaries rather than strict sequential kings, and adjust counting accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests Caranus and Perdiccas were contemporaries who erected small principalities later unified, recommending against assuming strict sequential reign-counting when sources hint at overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multiple lines of evidence over single-method reckoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on one method (e.g., generational counting); where other arguments exist (annals, synchronisms, anchored events), prefer the best-supported combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement: 'This method may be used alone, where other arguments are wanting; but where they are not wanting, the best arguments are to be preferred.' Combine inscriptional, annalistic, literary, and anchor-based evidence when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question implausibly long aggregated reign-lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject aggregate chronologies that imply implausible natural durations (e.g., seven kings reigning 244 continuous years) unless corroborated by strong evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises the calculation that seven Roman kings reigned 244 years in unbroken succession as 'much too long for the course of nature.' Use plausibility checks against demographic and historical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the testimony of local annals/translations for regional synchrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Where local records or translations of local annals exist (e.g., Tyrian annals translated by Menander), use them to synchronise local events with foreign chronologies (Hebrew, Greek).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Josephus' note that Tyrian annals were extant and translated is invoked to link the rapture of Europa and the friendship of Hiram and Solomon to the reigns of Tyrian kings. Such annals can provide precise internal sequences useful for cross-dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about assumptions and arithmetic when reconstructing intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing chronological proposals, show the arithmetic and assumptions (generation length, years per office, number of years shortened) used so readers can evaluate and replicate the reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the page the author makes explicit calculations (e.g., counting back X years from a given Olympiad, subtracting proportionally shortened years). Emulate this transparency in every reconstructed interval.
